claims.text: The starting material is a W–Cu composite containing tungsten particles or interconnected tungsten ligaments embedded in a copper matrix.
The tungsten surfaces can be coated with a continuous 10–20 nm nickel layer before consolidation.
Electroless plating or sputtering can produce the proposed nickel coating on preformed tungsten structures.
The nickel-coated tungsten structures can subsequently be infiltrated or co-sintered with copper.
A continuous nickel interlayer acts as a graded boundary between tungsten and copper.
The nickel interlayer improves bonding at the W–Cu interface.
The nickel interlayer reduces diffusional mismatch between tungsten and copper.
Nickel enhances wettability between tungsten and copper.
The nickel interlayer mitigates interfacial voids caused by thermal stresses.
The nickel interlayer mitigates interfacial voids caused by irradiation-induced atomic displacements.
The nickel interlayer reduces phase separation at the W–Cu interface.
Suppressing void formation and phase separation stabilizes the composite's thermally conductive network.
A more stable and continuous W–Ni–Cu interface lowers thermal contact resistance.
Nickel-coated W–Cu will have higher effective thermal conductivity than untreated W–Cu.
Nickel-coated W–Cu will undergo less thermal-performance degradation during cyclic thermal and irradiation exposure than untreated W–Cu.
Untreated W–Cu develops interfacial phase separation and voids under the proposed thermal and irradiation conditions.
Interfacial phase separation and voids degrade the thermal conductivity of untreated W–Cu.
The benefit of the nickel coating is expected to persist during thermal cycling up to approximately 700°C.
The benefit is expected to persist at irradiation doses typical of plasma-facing-material joint applications.
At substantially higher temperatures or extreme irradiation doses, the effectiveness of the nickel coating may diminish.
